newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR to chair talks on Bosnian refugee returns.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR to chair talks on Bosnian refugee returns.

text.p: Sadako Ogata, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, will chair high-level talks in Geneva on Monday to try to jump-start stalled refugee repatriations to former Yugoslavia, a spokeswoman said on Friday.
Carl Bildt, international High Representative to Bosnia, and John Kornblum, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs, will take part, according to U.N. and U.S. officials.
The meeting, which will also examine other humanitarian issues, will bring together immigration ministers from the region, representatives from donor countries and U.N. officials.
Nearly two million people remain displaced from the former Yugoslav republics a year after the signing of the Dayton peace accord which ended the 43-month war in Bosnia.
"We would like to turn the corner in 1997 and make it the summer of repatriation," a UNHCR spokeswoman told Reuters.
"But the problem of the return of minorities is a political problem which must be settled by the parties and the international community," she added.

Nudzeim Recica, Bosnian minister for refugees and displaced persons, Bratislava Morina, Serbian commissioner for refugees, and Ljubisa Vladusic, minister for refugees and displaced persons from the Bosnian Serb republic are expected to attend.
It was not yet clear who would represent Croatia.
At a peace review conference in London earlier this month, Western countries make clear that economic aid was tied to completing the terms of the peace accord.
Yet returnees face major hurdles, including lethal landmines, lack of homes and jobs, as well as refusal by local authorities to allow them to resettle in ethnic minority areas.
Only 250,000 have returned to their homes of origin, mostly to areas where their groups constitute an ethnic majority, according to the U.N. refugee agency.

On Thursday, U.N. human rights observers reported that minorities in Bosnia suffer "unchecked intimidation" in areas where they are not of the ethnic majority while movement is severly limited between Moslem, Croat and Serb areas in Bosnia.
The report also said evictions of Moslems and Serbs by Bosnian Croats in the divided southern city of Mostar had substantially increased local tensions.
